etymology: From the Greek anexichniastos, “that cannot be tracked out” or “past finding out,” joined to ploutos, “riches,” in Paul’s phrase for the wealth that is in Christ.
biblical_def: The unsearchable riches of Christ are the boundless treasures of grace, mercy, and glory laid up in the Son of God, which no creature can ever measure or exhaust. Paul, who counted himself less than the least of all saints, was given this grace, that he should preach among the Gentiles the unsearchable riches of Christ (Eph 3:8). The dictionary marks the word “unsearchable” as the very heart of the matter: the riches of Christ are not riches that may be reckoned up and brought to an end, but riches that the deepest searching of men and angels can never trace to their bottom. In Him are hid all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Col 2:3); in Him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily (Col 2:9); and of His fulness have all we received, and grace for grace (Joh 1:16). So the Scripture teaches that the believer is made rich, not with the perishing wealth of this world, but with an inheritance incorruptible, undefiled, and that fadeth not away (1Pe 1:4), bought by the blood of the Son and kept by the power of God. These riches are unsearchable because they are the riches of an infinite Christ, freely given to the poor in spirit; and the office of the preacher is to spend his life in displaying a wealth he can never come to the end of, that sinners may forsake their beggary and be made heirs of God, and joint-heirs with Christ.
webster_summary: The boundless and unfathomable treasures of grace and glory laid up in Christ for His people.
webster_full: THE UNSEARCHABLE RICHES, the treasures of grace and glory in Christ which cannot be measured.
The word “unsearchable” means that cannot be tracked out or found to the bottom.
Paul was given grace to preach these riches among the Gentiles.
In Christ are hid all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge.
The believer is made rich with an inheritance incorruptible and undefiled.

corruption_summary: A treasure of Scripture; the unfathomable wealth of Christ, freely given to the poor in spirit who come to Him.
corruption_paragraphs: The unsearchable riches of Christ have drawn little redefinition from the present age, the phrase surviving chiefly as a comfort to believers. The dictionary records it that the reader may mark the boundless wealth of the Son which the preacher is set to display and the saint to inherit.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that all true riches are laid up in Christ, and in Him alone. The world counts its wealth in goods that perish and a glory that fades; but in Christ are hid all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge, and of His fulness the believer receives grace for grace. These riches are unsearchable because they are the riches of an infinite Saviour, and the soul that has Christ has an inheritance incorruptible and undefiled. Let the reader forsake the beggary of the world and be made an heir of God in His Son.
roots_summary: From the Greek for “that cannot be tracked out,” the phrase names the unfathomable wealth of Christ.

etymology: From the Greek koinonia, “fellowship” or “sharing,” joined to pathema, “suffering,” in Paul’s desire to share the sufferings of Christ.
biblical_def: The fellowship of His sufferings is that communion with Christ in affliction by which the believer is conformed to his crucified Lord, and so made partaker also of His resurrection life. Paul, having counted all things but loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus his Lord, breathed out this great longing: That I may know him, and the power of his resurrection, and the fellowship of his sufferings, being made conformable unto his death (Phil 3:10). The dictionary marks this phrase as the heart of the Christian’s union with Christ: to know Christ is not only to be saved by His sufferings, but to be joined to Him in them, to fill up that which is behind of the afflictions of Christ in the flesh, for His body’s sake, which is the church (Col 1:24). So the Scripture teaches that if we suffer with Him, we shall also be glorified together (Rom 8:17); for the order is fixed, the cross before the crown, the death before the rising. The believer does not earn his salvation by suffering, for the atonement was finished upon the cross; but being united to Christ by faith, he is made like Him, sharing the reproach, the loss, and the affliction of his Master in this present age. And this fellowship is no mere sorrow, for it is fellowship, communion with a living Christ who suffered and now reigns; and the soul that shares His sufferings shall surely share His glory.
webster_summary: The believer’s communion with Christ in affliction, by which he is conformed to his Lord and partakes of His resurrection.
webster_full: THE FELLOWSHIP OF HIS SUFFERINGS, communion with Christ in affliction, conforming the believer to his Lord.
Paul counted all things loss that he might know Christ and this fellowship.
To suffer with Christ is to be made conformable unto His death.
If we suffer with Him, we shall also be glorified together.
The order is fixed: the cross before the crown, the death before the rising.

corruption_summary: A treasure of Scripture; the believer’s union with his crucified Lord in suffering, which goes before the sharing of His glory.
corruption_paragraphs: The fellowship of His sufferings has drawn little redefinition from the present age, surviving as a phrase of deep comfort to the afflicted saint. The dictionary records it that the reader may mark the union with Christ that joins the believer to his Lord in suffering as truly as in glory.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that union with Christ means conformity to His death before participation in His glory. The believer is not saved by his sufferings, for the atonement was finished upon the cross; yet being joined to Christ by faith, he is made like Him, bearing the reproach and affliction of his Master in this present age. If we suffer with Him, we shall also be glorified together; the cross goes before the crown. Let the suffering saint know that his afflictions are not a sign of God’s desertion but the very mark of his fellowship with a living and reigning Christ.
roots_summary: From the Greek for “fellowship in suffering,” the phrase names communion with Christ in His afflictions.
roots_lines: The Fellowship of His Sufferings — Greek koinonia ton pathematon, “sharing in the sufferings.”
It is communion with Christ in affliction, not a price paid for salvation.

It goes before the sharing of Christ’s resurrection and glory.
usage: To know Christ is to be joined to Him in His sufferings as well as His glory.
If we suffer with Him, we shall also be glorified together.
The afflictions of the saint are the very mark of his fellowship with his Lord.

word: The Prize of the High Calling
etymology: From the Greek brabeion, “the prize awarded to the victor,” joined to the upward (ano) calling of God in Christ Jesus.
biblical_def: The prize of the high calling is the crown of glory set before the believer at the end of his course, toward which he presses with all his strength in this present race. Paul, the great runner, would have none think he had already attained or were already perfect; rather he said, I press toward the mark for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus (Phil 3:14). The dictionary marks the figure as drawn from the games: the runner, forgetting those things which are behind, reaching forth unto those things which are before, presses with straining body toward the goal, that he may obtain the prize. So the Scripture teaches that the Christian life is no idle profession but a race to be run with patience (Heb 12:1), a fight to be fought, a course to be finished, a crown to be won. Yet the prize is not earned as wages, for it is the prize of a high calling, the upward and heavenly calling of God, and it is in Christ Jesus, given of grace to them whom God has effectually called. There is laid up a crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, shall give at that day to all them also that love His appearing (2Ti 4:8). The believer therefore runs not in uncertainty, but presses toward a sure reward, that he may lay hold on that for which also he is laid hold of by Christ.
webster_summary: The crown of glory set before the believer, toward which he presses in the upward calling of God in Christ.
webster_full: THE PRIZE OF THE HIGH CALLING, the crown of glory set before the believer at the end of his race.
The figure is drawn from the games, where the runner presses toward the goal.
Paul pressed toward the mark, forgetting the things behind.
The calling is high, upward, and heavenly, and it is in Christ Jesus.
There is laid up a crown of righteousness for them that love His appearing.

corruption_summary: A treasure of Scripture; the crown of glory toward which the believer presses, given of grace in the upward calling of God.
corruption_paragraphs: The prize of the high calling has drawn little redefinition from the present age, surviving as a spur to perseverance in the Christian race. The dictionary records it that the reader may mark the goal and reward set before every runner whom God has called in Christ.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the Christian life is a race to be run to the end, pressing toward a sure prize. The believer does not run in uncertainty, nor earn the crown as wages, for it is the prize of a high and heavenly calling, given of grace in Christ Jesus. Forgetting the things behind, he reaches forth to the things before, that he may lay hold on that for which also he is laid hold of by Christ. Let the reader not loiter as one who has already attained, but press toward the mark, for a crown of righteousness is laid up for all that love His appearing.
roots_summary: From the Greek for “the victor’s prize,” the phrase names the crown of glory in the upward calling of God.
roots_lines: The Prize of the High Calling — Greek brabeion, “the prize awarded to the victor.”

etymology: From the Greek eirene, “peace” (answering to the Hebrew shalom, “wholeness, well-being”), the settled tranquillity of soul which God gives through Christ.
biblical_def: The peace of God is that holy calm and settled rest of soul which God bestows upon His people through Christ, keeping their hearts amid every care and fear. Paul bids the saints be careful for nothing, but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving to let their requests be made known unto God; and then comes the promise: And the peace of God, which passeth all understanding, shall keep your hearts and minds through Christ Jesus (Phil 4:7). The dictionary marks this peace as a gift, not an achievement, and as a guardian, not a feeling only; for the word rendered “keep” is a soldier’s word, that the peace of God shall garrison the heart as a watch about a city. It passeth all understanding, for it is not the peace the world gives, which is bottomed on outward ease, but a peace that abides in tribulation, in want, in the prison, and at the stake. So the Scripture teaches that this peace flows from peace with God, made by the blood of the cross; for being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ (Rom 5:1). The Lord Himself bequeathed it: Peace I leave with you, my peace I give unto you: not as the world giveth, give I unto you (Joh 14:27). It is therefore Christ’s own peace, lodged in the believer by His Spirit, ruling the heart and stilling the storm of care.
webster_summary: The settled tranquillity of soul which God gives through Christ, garrisoning the heart against all care and fear.
webster_full: THE PEACE OF GOD, the settled calm of soul which God bestows through Christ.
It passeth all understanding and keeps the heart and mind.
The word “keep” is a soldier’s word, to garrison as a watch.
It flows from peace with God made by the blood of the cross.
It is Christ’s own peace, not as the world giveth.

corruption_summary: A treasure of Scripture; the settled rest of soul God gives through Christ, flowing from peace made by His blood.
corruption_paragraphs: The peace of God has drawn little redefinition from the present age, surviving as a comfort named in many a believer’s prayer. The dictionary records it that the reader may mark its true ground in peace with God, made by the blood of the cross, and not in mere outward ease.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the peace of God is a gift of grace, garrisoning the heart, and not a mood the soul works up in itself. It passeth all understanding because it abides where the world’s peace fails, in want and tribulation and at the stake; for it flows from peace with God through justification by faith in Christ. The world offers a peace bottomed on circumstance; Christ gives His own peace, lodged in the heart by His Spirit. Let the anxious soul cast its care upon God in prayer with thanksgiving, and the peace of God shall keep the heart and mind through Christ Jesus.
roots_summary: From the Greek eirene, answering the Hebrew shalom, the phrase names the soul’s rest given by God in Christ.
roots_lines: The Peace of God — Greek eirene, the Hebrew shalom, “wholeness and well-being.”
It passeth all understanding, surpassing every earthly calm.
It keeps the heart and mind as a garrison keeps a city.

It is Christ’s own peace, not as the world giveth.

etymology: From the Greek nous, “mind” or “understanding” (1Co 2:16), and phroneo, “to be minded, to set the mind” (Phil 2:5), naming the Spirit-given understanding and lowly disposition of the believer in Christ.
biblical_def: The mind of Christ is the Spirit-given understanding and the lowly, self-emptying disposition which belong to the believer who is united to his Lord. Paul declares of the spiritual man, We have the mind of Christ (1Co 2:16); for the natural man receiveth not the things of the Spirit of God, neither can he know them, but the believer, taught of the Spirit, judges all things by the light of Christ. The dictionary marks two threads woven into this treasure. The first is understanding: the things of God are spiritually discerned, and the believer, given the Spirit, has the very mind by which to know the deep things of God which He hath revealed (1Co 2:10). The second is disposition: Let this mind be in you, which was also in Christ Jesus (Phil 2:5); who, being in the form of God, made Himself of no reputation, took upon Him the form of a servant, and humbled Himself, and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross (Phil 2:7, 2:8). So the Scripture teaches that to have the mind of Christ is both to think God’s thoughts after Him and to walk in Christ’s lowliness, esteeming others better than ourselves. This mind is not native to fallen man, who is enmity against God; it is the gift of regeneration, wrought by the Spirit who renews the understanding and bends the will to the pattern of the meek and lowly Saviour.
webster_summary: The Spirit-given understanding and lowly disposition of the believer united to Christ, both to know God and to walk in Christ’s meekness.
webster_full: THE MIND OF CHRIST, the Spirit-given understanding and lowly disposition of the believer in Christ.
The spiritual man has the mind of Christ to discern the things of God.
The natural man cannot know the things of the Spirit of God.
Believers are bidden to let the lowly mind of Christ be in them.
Christ humbled Himself and became obedient unto the death of the cross.
scriptures: For who hath known the mind of the Lord, that he may instruct him? But we have the mind of Christ.

corruption_summary: A treasure of Scripture; the Spirit-given understanding and lowliness of Christ, granted to the believer in regeneration.
corruption_paragraphs: The mind of Christ has drawn little redefinition from the present age, surviving as a phrase for both spiritual understanding and Christlike humility. The dictionary records it that the reader may mark its two threads, the discerning of God’s things and the lowly disposition of the Saviour.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the mind of Christ is the gift of regeneration, not the achievement of nature. The natural man cannot know the things of the Spirit, for they are spiritually discerned; only the believer, renewed by the Spirit, has the mind by which to know the deep things of God. And the same mind is a lowly mind: let this mind be in you, which was also in Christ Jesus, who made Himself of no reputation and was obedient unto death. To have Christ’s mind is to think God’s thoughts after Him and to walk in His meekness, esteeming others better than ourselves.
roots_summary: From the Greek nous and phroneo, the phrase names the believer’s Spirit-given understanding and lowly mind in Christ.
roots_lines: The Mind of Christ — Greek nous Christou, “the mind of Christ” (1Co 2:16).
The verb phroneo, “to be minded,” frames the lowly mind of Phil 2:5.
It is the Spirit-given understanding by which God’s things are discerned.

word: The Old Man and the New Man
etymology: From the Greek palaios anthropos, “the old man,” and kainos anthropos, “the new man,” naming the corrupt nature inherited from Adam and the renewed nature created in Christ.
biblical_def: The old man and the new man are Paul’s names for the two natures set before the believer in the work of sanctification: the corrupt old self inherited from Adam, and the renewed self created in Christ. Paul bids the saints put off concerning the former conversation the old man, which is corrupt according to the deceitful lusts; and be renewed in the spirit of their mind; and put on the new man, which after God is created in righteousness and true holiness (Eph 4:22, 4:23, 4:24). Again he says they have put off the old man with his deeds, and have put on the new man, which is renewed in knowledge after the image of him that created him (Col 3:9, 3:10). The dictionary marks the ground of this duty in the cross: knowing this, that our old man is crucified with him, that the body of sin might be destroyed, that henceforth we should not serve sin (Rom 6:6). So the Scripture teaches that in regeneration the believer is made a new creature, the old having been judged and crucified with Christ; and in sanctification he daily mortifies the old man’s remaining corruptions and puts on the new man’s graces. This is no mere turning over of a new leaf, nor the polishing of fallen nature, but the death of the old self in union with the crucified Christ, and the rising of a new self created after the image of God in righteousness and true holiness.
webster_summary: Paul’s names for the corrupt nature inherited from Adam, crucified with Christ, and the renewed nature created in Christ unto holiness.
webster_full: THE OLD MAN AND THE NEW MAN, the corrupt Adamic nature and the renewed nature created in Christ.
The old man is corrupt according to the deceitful lusts and must be put off.
The new man is created after God in righteousness and true holiness.
Our old man is crucified with Christ, that the body of sin be destroyed.
This is the death of the old self and the rising of a new in Christ.

corruption_paragraphs: The old man and the new man have drawn little redefinition from the present age, surviving as the plain language of mortification and renewal. The dictionary records them that the reader may mark the death of the old self in union with Christ and the rising of the new self created after the image of God.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that sanctification is not the improving of fallen nature but the crucifying of the old man and the putting on of the new. Our old man is crucified with Christ, that the body of sin might be destroyed; and the new man is created after God in righteousness and true holiness. This is no turning over of a new leaf, nor the polishing of the old self, but the death of the Adamic nature in union with the crucified Lord, and a daily mortifying of its remaining corruptions while the graces of the new man are put on. Let no man think to mend the old man; he must be put off, and the new man put on.
roots_summary: From the Greek palaios and kainos anthropos, the phrase names the old Adamic self and the new self in Christ.
roots_lines: The Old Man and the New Man — Greek palaios and kainos anthropos.

It is crucified with Christ, that the body of sin be destroyed.
The new man is created after God in righteousness and true holiness.
Sanctification puts off the one and puts on the other daily.

etymology: From the Greek anakainosis, “a making new again, renovation,” joined to nous, “mind,” in Paul’s call to be transformed in the understanding.
biblical_def: The renewing of the mind is the inward work of the Holy Ghost by which the understanding of the believer is made new, that he may discern and delight in the will of God. Paul beseeches the brethren, by the mercies of God, that they present their bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable unto God, which is their reasonable service; and then he sets the great commandment: And be not conformed to this world: but be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind, that ye may prove what is that good, and acceptable, and perfect, will of God (Rom 12:2). The dictionary marks the word “transformed,” which is the word for a thorough change of inward form, not the donning of an outward fashion; the believer is not to be pressed into the mould of this present age, but inwardly remade. So the Scripture teaches that sanctification begins in the mind, for as a man thinketh in his heart, so is he (Pro 23:7); the will follows the understanding, and the life follows the will. This renewing is no work of unaided man, who by nature is darkened in his understanding (Eph 4:18); it is the renewing of the Holy Ghost (Tit 3:5), wrought by the washing of regeneration and carried on through the Word, that the believer may prove in his daily walk the good and perfect will of God.
webster_summary: The Spirit’s inward work of making the believer’s understanding new, that he may discern and delight in the will of God.
webster_full: THE RENEWING OF THE MIND, the Spirit’s making new of the believer’s understanding.
The word “transformed” means a thorough inward change of form.
The believer is not to be conformed to the mould of this world.
Sanctification begins in the mind, for the will follows the understanding.
It is the renewing of the Holy Ghost, wrought through the Word.

corruption_paragraphs: The renewing of the mind has drawn little redefinition from the present age, surviving as a phrase for inward transformation. The dictionary records it that the reader may mark its true author, the Holy Ghost, and its true ground, the regenerating mercy of God, lest it be reduced to a mere bettering of one’s thoughts by human effort.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that sanctification begins in the mind, and the renewing of the mind is the Spirit’s work, not man’s. The believer is not pressed into the mould of this world but inwardly transformed, that he may prove the good and perfect will of God. By nature the understanding is darkened and at enmity with God; it is made new by the washing of regeneration and the renewing of the Holy Ghost, carried on through the Word. Let the reader yield his understanding to be remade by the Spirit, that the will and the walk may follow the renewed mind into the will of God.
roots_summary: From the Greek anakainosis nous, the phrase names the Spirit’s making new of the believer’s understanding.
roots_lines: The Renewing of the Mind — Greek anakainosis tou noos, “renovation of the mind.”
The verb “transformed” means a thorough change of inward form.

Sanctification begins in the mind, for the will follows the understanding.

etymology: From the Greek arrhabon, “earnest, pledge, down-payment” (a Semitic loanword), naming the Holy Spirit given as the first instalment and surety of the believer’s inheritance.
biblical_def: The earnest of the Spirit is the Holy Ghost given to the believer as the pledge and down-payment of his promised inheritance, the first instalment that secures the whole. An earnest, in the speech of the merchant, was a portion of the price paid beforehand, both as a token of good faith and as a binding surety that all the rest should follow. So God, having sealed His people, hath given the earnest of the Spirit in their hearts (2Co 1:22); and again, He that hath wrought us for the selfsame thing is God, who also hath given unto us the earnest of the Spirit (2Co 5:5). Paul names the same gift in another place: that holy Spirit of promise, which is the earnest of our inheritance until the redemption of the purchased possession, unto the praise of His glory (Eph 1:14). The dictionary marks this as the great ground of the saints’ perseverance: the Spirit is not only the seal that marks them as God’s, but the earnest that guarantees their final glory. So the Scripture teaches that the believer is kept, not by his own strength, but by the indwelling Spirit who is God’s own pledge that He will finish what He has begun. He which hath begun a good work in you will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ (Phil 1:6); for the down-payment is from God Himself, and God forfeits no pledge.
webster_summary: The Holy Spirit given to the believer as the pledge and down-payment securing his promised inheritance.
webster_full: THE EARNEST OF THE SPIRIT, the Holy Ghost given as the pledge of the believer’s inheritance.
An earnest is a portion of the price paid beforehand as surety.

It is the ground of the saints’ perseverance, for God forfeits no pledge.

Phil 1:6
Being confident of this very thing, that he which hath begun a good work in you will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ:
corruption_summary: A treasure of Scripture; the Spirit given as God’s pledge of the inheritance, the great ground of the saints’ perseverance.
corruption_paragraphs: The earnest of the Spirit has drawn little redefinition from the present age, surviving as a phrase of assurance to the believer. The dictionary records it that the reader may mark the Spirit as God’s own pledge and down-payment, securing the whole inheritance He has promised.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the perseverance of the saints, grounded not in the believer’s strength but in the indwelling Spirit given as God’s earnest. An earnest is the down-payment that binds the giver to pay all the rest; and God, having sealed His people and given the earnest of the Spirit in their hearts, has pledged Himself to redeem the purchased possession. He which hath begun a good work will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ. Let the trembling believer rest here: the surety of his glory is not his own grip on God, but God’s pledge, who forfeits nothing He has begun.
roots_summary: From the Greek arrhabon, “earnest or pledge,” the phrase names the Spirit as the surety of the inheritance.

It is the great ground of the saints’ perseverance unto glory.
usage: God hath sealed us, and given the earnest of the Spirit in our hearts.

etymology: From the Greek anekdiegetos, “that cannot be fully told or declared,” joined to dorea, “gift,” in Paul’s thanksgiving for the gift of God in Christ.
biblical_def: The unspeakable gift is the gift of God’s own Son, Christ Jesus, so great and so far beyond all telling that the apostle can only break forth in thanksgiving: Thanks be unto God for his unspeakable gift (2Co 9:15). The dictionary marks the word “unspeakable,” which means not a gift unworthy to be spoken of, but a gift that cannot be fully declared, surpassing all the speech of men and angels. Paul has been teaching the grace of giving, and the cheerful, bountiful liberality God loves in His people; and he crowns the whole with the supreme example, the gift of the Son, beside which every gift of ours is small. For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life (Joh 3:16); and He that spared not His own Son, but delivered Him up for us all, how shall He not with Him also freely give us all things? (Rom 8:32). So the Scripture teaches that the fountain of all grace is the giving of Christ, the gift that includes all other gifts; for in giving the Son, God gave righteousness, reconciliation, the Spirit, the inheritance, and Himself. This gift is unspeakable because it is the gift of an infinite love at an infinite cost, freely bestowed on the unworthy; and the only fit answer of the redeemed is the everlasting thanks the apostle here pours out.
webster_summary: God’s gift of His own Son, Christ Jesus, so great it cannot be fully told, the fountain of all other gifts.

corruption_paragraphs: The unspeakable gift has drawn little redefinition from the present age, surviving as a phrase of thanksgiving for the gift of Christ. The dictionary records it that the reader may mark the gift that cannot be fully told, the Son of God given at infinite cost to the unworthy.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the gift of Christ is the fountain of all grace, including all other gifts in itself. God spared not His own Son, but delivered Him up for us all; and He that gave the Son will with Him freely give us all things. This gift is unspeakable, surpassing all the speech of men and angels, for it is the gift of an infinite love at an infinite cost. The only fit answer is the everlasting thanks the apostle pours out, and a life given back to the God who first gave His Son for sinners.

etymology: From the Greek parathēkē, “a thing committed in trust, a deposit” (from paratithēmi, “to set before, to entrust”), naming the sound doctrine committed to the believer to be guarded.
biblical_def: The good deposit is the treasure of sound doctrine and the gospel committed in trust to the believer, which he is charged to keep safe by the power of the Holy Ghost. Paul charges Timothy, his son in the faith: That good thing which was committed unto thee keep by the Holy Ghost which dwelleth in us (2Ti 1:14). The word he uses is the merchant’s word for a deposit, a thing laid up in another’s hands to be kept whole and rendered up untouched. Just before, the apostle had set his own example: I know whom I have believed, and am persuaded that he is able to keep that which I have committed unto him against that day (2Ti 1:12). So there are two deposits answering each other. The believer commits his soul to Christ, who is able to keep it; and Christ commits to the believer the good thing of sound doctrine, which he is to guard. The dictionary marks this as the charge of every faithful minister and church: the form of sound words (2Ti 1:13), the faith once delivered unto the saints (Jude 1:3), is not the church’s to amend, lessen, or improve, but a sacred trust to be held fast and handed on unaltered. So the Scripture teaches the closed and finished deposit of revealed truth, guarded against every novelty and corruption; and the guarding is not by human cleverness but by the Holy Ghost who dwelleth in us.
webster_summary: The sound doctrine and gospel committed in trust to the believer, to be kept whole by the Holy Ghost.

corruption_summary: A treasure of Scripture; the sound doctrine entrusted to the church to be guarded whole and handed on unaltered.
corruption_paragraphs: The good deposit has drawn little redefinition from the present age as a phrase, though the trust it names is ever under assault. The dictionary records it that the reader may mark the charge to keep the sound doctrine committed to the church, neither amending nor lessening it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the faith once delivered to the saints is a fixed and finished deposit, the church’s to guard and hand on, not to amend or improve. The form of sound words is a sacred trust, laid up in the believer’s hands to be kept whole and rendered up untouched against that day. This guarding is not by human cleverness but by the Holy Ghost who dwelleth in us. Let the reader hold fast the deposit against every novelty and corruption, and earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints.
